Cigarette demand in US states, 1963-1992 (Baltagi and Levin)

Source: R/data-cigar.R
cigar.Rd

The classic real public panel of cigarette consumption, prices and income for 46 US states (45 states plus the District of Columbia; Alaska, Colorado, Hawaii, North Carolina and Oregon are not included) observed every year from 1963 to 1992 (30 years), used by Baltagi and Levin (1986, 1992) and in Baltagi's textbook to estimate a dynamic demand equation for an addictive good. The panel is balanced with no missing values. The first nine columns are the original file; the last four are the log variables of the textbook equation ln C(it) = a + b1 ln C(i,t-1) + b2 ln P(it) + b3 ln Pn(it) + b4 ln Y(it) + u(it). The build script, with the validation against the published estimates, is data-raw/cigar.R in the package's GitHub repository.

Usage

cigar

Format

A data frame with 1,380 rows (46 states x 30 years) and 13 columns. The panel index pair is (state, year).

state

factor, two-letter US state abbreviation (46 levels, DC for the District of Columbia); the panel individual index

year

integer calendar year, 1963-1992; the panel time index

price

numeric, average retail price per pack of cigarettes, cents, nominal (taxes included)

pop

numeric, state population, thousands

pop16

numeric, population of smoking age, thousands (labelled "population above the age of 16" in the data archive; the textbook describes smoking age as 14 and older)

cpi

numeric, consumer price index, 1983 = 100

ndi

numeric, per capita disposable income, dollars, nominal

sales

numeric, cigarette sales, packs per head of total population

pimin

numeric, minimum price per pack in adjoining states, cents, nominal (proxy for casual smuggling across state borders)

lnc

numeric, log real per capita consumption by persons of smoking age, log(sales * pop / pop16)

lnp

numeric, log real price, log(price / cpi * 100) (1983 cents)

lnpn

numeric, log real minimum neighbouring-state price, log(pimin / cpi * 100)

lny

numeric, log real per capita disposable income, log(ndi / cpi * 100) (1983 dollars)

Source

File Cigar.txt of the data archive of Baltagi, Econometric Analysis of Panel Data (Wiley companion site), https://www.wiley.com/legacy/wileychi/baltagi/supp/Cigar.txt, listed at https://www.wiley.com/legacy/wileychi/baltagi/datasets.html, downloaded 2026-11-01. The original variables are identical to the copies distributed under GPL (>= 2) in the CRAN packages plm (plm::Cigar) and Ecdat (Ecdat::Cigar), which trace the data to the same archive; this package redistributes it on the same terms. The underlying series are public statistics (Tobacco Institute, The Tax Burden on Tobacco; US Census population estimates; consumer price index and personal income series). Cite Baltagi and Levin (1992) and Baltagi (2005) when using the data.

Teaching use

  • How habit forming is smoking, and what are the short- and long-run price elasticities? Dynamic demand lnc ~ lag(lnc, 1) + lnp + lnpn + lny: pooled OLS (panglm(model = "pooling")) overstates persistence because the state effect sits in the lagged outcome; two-way within (model = "within", effect = "twoways") understates it (Nickell bias, of order 1 / T); Arellano-Bond difference GMM and Blundell-Bond system GMM (pangmm() with transformation = "d" or "ld") are consistent for fixed T. A credible GMM estimate of the lag coefficient lies between the within (0.83) and pooled (0.97) values. The long-run elasticity is b2 / (1 - b1).

  • How much do the GMM results depend on the instrument set? With N = 46 states the full Arellano-Bond instrument matrix has 437 columns; compare collapse = TRUE and maxlag, and read the Hansen test (it is uninformative, p close to 1, when instruments proliferate) and the AR(2) test.

  • Does cross-border bootlegging matter? The coefficient of the neighbouring-state price lnpn in the static and dynamic models.

  • Static demand: fixed versus random state effects for lnc ~ lnp + lnpn + lny, panglm() with model = "within" and "random", and panhausman(). Here the classical contrast V_fe - V_re is not positive definite (the classical statistic is negative), so use the regression-based method = "mundlak" version, which rejects random effects (F = 7.17 on 3 and 45 df).

  • Initial conditions: the Wooldridge dynamic correlated random effects model (panglm(dynamic = TRUE)), here a contrast with GMM because the state-effect variance is estimated at zero once the initial outcome is conditioned on.

References

Baltagi, B. H. and Levin, D. (1986). Estimating dynamic demand for cigarettes using panel data: the effects of bootlegging, taxation and advertising reconsidered. Review of Economics and Statistics, 68(1), 148-155.

Baltagi, B. H. and Levin, D. (1992). Cigarette taxation: raising revenues and reducing consumption. Structural Change and Economic Dynamics, 3(2), 321-335.

Baltagi, B. H., Griffin, J. M. and Xiong, W. (2000). To pool or not to pool: homogeneous versus heterogeneous estimators applied to cigarette demand. Review of Economics and Statistics, 82(1), 117-126.

Baltagi, B. H. (2005). Econometric Analysis of Panel Data, 3rd edition. Wiley. Section 8.8, Table 8.1 (Pooled estimation results, cigarette demand equation 1963-92) and Table 8.2 (Arellano-Bond estimates).

Arellano, M. and Bond, S. (1991). Some tests of specification for panel data: Monte Carlo evidence and an application to employment equations. Review of Economic Studies, 58(2), 277-297.

Nickell, S. (1981). Biases in dynamic models with fixed effects. Econometrica, 49(6), 1417-1426.

Examples

data(cigar)
ix <- c("state", "year")
f <- lnc ~ lag(lnc, 1) + lnp + lnpn + lny

## Baltagi (2005), Table 8.1: OLS, two-way within and one-step
## Arellano-Bond GMM
ols <- panglm(f, data = cigar, index = ix, model = "pooling")
fe  <- panglm(f, data = cigar, index = ix, model = "within",
              effect = "twoways")
ab1 <- pangmm(lnc ~ lag(lnc, 1) + lnp + lnpn + lny | lag(lnc, 2:99),
              data = cigar, index = ix, transformation = "d",
              model = "onestep")
#> Warning: 437 instruments for 46 individuals: too many instruments bias GMM toward OLS and weaken the Hansen test; use collapse = TRUE or a smaller maxlag
round(rbind(OLS = coef(ols)[-1], Within = coef(fe),
            "GMM one-step" = coef(ab1)[1:4]), 3)
#>              lag(lnc, 1)    lnp   lnpn    lny
#> OLS                0.969 -0.090  0.024 -0.031
#> Within             0.833 -0.299  0.034  0.100
#> GMM one-step       0.843 -0.377 -0.016  0.139
## published: 0.97 -0.090 0.024 -0.03 / 0.83 -0.299 0.034 0.10 /
##            0.84 -0.377 -0.016 0.14

## long-run price elasticity, b2 / (1 - b1)
lr <- function(b) b[["lnp"]] / (1 - b[[1]])
c(within = lr(coef(fe)), gmm = lr(coef(ab1)))
#>    within       gmm 
#> -1.792118 -2.400697 

## collapsed instruments: system GMM, two-step, Windmeijer errors
sys <- pangmm(lnc ~ lag(lnc, 1) + lnp + lnpn + lny | lag(lnc, 2:99),
              data = cigar, index = ix, transformation = "ld",
              model = "twostep", collapse = TRUE, maxlag = 6)
summary(sys)
#> 
#> Call:
#> pangmm(formula = lnc ~ lag(lnc, 1) + lnp + lnpn + lny | lag(lnc, 
#>     2:99), data = cigar, index = ix, transformation = "ld", model = "twostep", 
#>     collapse = TRUE, maxlag = 6)
#> 
#> Estimator: two-way two-step system GMM (Blundell-Bond) 
#> n = 2622  groups = 46  T = 30  instruments = 41 
#> vcov: robust (Windmeijer) 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> lag(lnc, 1)  0.75944    0.09332   8.138 4.03e-16 ***
#> lnp         -0.34842    0.06377  -5.464 4.65e-08 ***
#> lnpn         0.02046    0.05601   0.365    0.715    
#> lny          0.07448    0.05270   1.413    0.158    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Arellano-Bond AR(1) test: z = -4.438, p = 9.093e-06
#> Arellano-Bond AR(2) test: z = 1.403, p = 0.1607
#> Sargan test (not robust): chi2(8) = 44.42, p = 4.734e-07
#> Hansen J test (robust): chi2(8) = 17.81, p = 0.0227
#> Wald test for coefficients: chi2(4) = 365.3, p = < 2.2e-16
#> 

## static demand: fixed vs random state effects (regression-based
## Mundlak version of the Hausman test, robust to serial correlation)
sfe <- panglm(lnc ~ lnp + lnpn + lny, data = cigar, index = ix,
              model = "within")
panhausman(sfe, method = "mundlak", data = cigar)
#> 
#> 	Mundlak specification test (fixed vs. random effects), vcov: cluster
#> 
#> F = 7.172, df = 3, 45, p-value = 0.0004902
#> Wald chisq = 21.52, df = 3, p-value = 8.228e-05
#> alternative hypothesis: one model is inconsistent
#>
